newsitem.title: JAPAN: Peru crisis prods Japan to rethink mission safety.
newsitem.headline: Peru crisis prods Japan to rethink mission safety.

text.p: The seizure of the Japanese ambassador's residence in Peru with hundreds of hostages has raised new questions about Japan's security safeguards for its diplomats abroad, analysts said on Thursday.

Security at Japan's 182 embassies and other missions overseas has been beefed up considerably in recent years in step with Japan's growing global profile and rising awareness of the dangers lurking abroad.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto rebuffed calls from government circles for hefty increases in its embassy security budget, which is expected to reach 19.3 billion yen ($169 million) in 1997, nearly double 1992 levels.
"If a terrorist group intrudes, it is the responsibility of the country that is guarding outside... If such an incident occurs in Japan, it would be Japan's responsibility," he said.

But critics say Japan's security awareness lags behind that of other powers, hampered by a lack of intelligence gathering expertise, constitutional restraints and even by Tokyo's relative lack of experience with violent crime at home.

Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda acknowledged that safeguards were less than perfect on Tuesday night in Lima, when a dozen or so rebels from the Cuban-inspired Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) stormed the official residence during a reception to mark the emperor's birthday.
"I do not intend to insist that security was perfect," Ikeda told a news conference on Wednesday night as his ministry rushed to compile information on the unfolding crisis.

Japan, a staunch backer of President Alberto Fujimori's government, believed Lima had all but won its 16-year war on communist rebels belonging to the MRTA and the larger and better-known Maoist Shining Path, experts said.
"Japanese diplomats in Lima took lax security measures because they believed guerrilla or terrorist activities were subsiding," said Hideaki Kase, an international diplomacy analyst and author.
Ikeda, who left for Lima on Thursday, stressed the immediate priority of securing the safety of hostages.
But other foreign ministry officials, using a crisis operation room for the first time since it was built six years ago, faced tough questions about mission security.

In 1993, Japan's embassy in Lima was slammed by a car bomb and destroyed in an attack attributed to leftists. As a result, the Lima mission joined the list of the most heavily guarded among Japan's government missions overseas, officials said.

The Japanese Embassy and the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima are protected by three security officers from Japan's National Police Agency, three or four guards from a Japanese security company and four Peruvian policemen with two patrol cars, officials said.

But the lightly armed patrolmen were no match for the MRTA fighters, who wielded machine guns and grenades as they swept into the residence during the reception. They were reported to have helpers inside disguised as waiters.
The guerrillas cut all telephones at the residence and even found the supposedly secret phone lines, limiting Tokyo's access to its diplomats to several mobile phones.
"It looks as though the criminals outsmarted us," a senior foreign ministry official was quoted as saying.

"Security measures taken by Japan are a far cry from those by the United States, which posts Marines on full alert in its embassies worldwide while Japan uses only one or a few police officers at each embassy," Kase told Reuters.

"It would be safer if Japan sends its Self-Defence Forces (military) personnel, but to do so Japan must change its constitution," Kase said, referring to Japan's post World War Two bar on sending troops overseas.($=114 yen)
